messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Leilani, a twenty-year-old interior designer, remembers the evening vividly, though often the details blur into a terrifying rush of pure sensation. She had been at home with her then-boyfriend, an argument simmering beneath the surface of their quiet apartment. It escalated quickly, his voice rising, growing louder and more menacing with each word. She tried to back away, to create space, but he had cornered her in the dimly lit living room, the shadows deepening around them as the sun set. The sudden, explosive crack of his hand against her face, followed by the sickening thud of her head against the wall, was the last clear thing she recalled before a haze of fear and pain took over. She was alone with him, trapped, the noise of his rage filling the small space. Even now, when she attempts to recount the full story to her husband or a trusted friend, Leilani finds herself losing the thread, the words catching in her throat, unable to articulate the sequence of events with clarity.

In the months that followed, Leilani found her world shrinking. The constant, gnawing feeling that her life had been destroyed by the trauma settled deep within her, a belief that colored every interaction and decision. She had come to feel she no longer belonged anywhere, adrift from the person she once was and disconnected from those around her. A profound mistrust of people, especially men, had taken root, making her wary and guarded. She was certain that anyone could turn, that the world was inherently unsafe. This conviction was reinforced by a body that felt constantly tense, always ready to react to danger. Her hypervigilance became second nature; she was superalert, watchful, and on guard, particularly in public spaces. She frequently found herself looking behind her, checking if someone was following, a nervous habit that intensified with every unexpected sound.

Her occupation as an interior designer, which once brought her joy, became a minefield of triggers. Loud noises, an unavoidable part of construction sites or bustling showrooms, would send a jolt of terror through her, immediately transporting her back to the apartment, the sound of his voice ringing in her ears. Being alone with men, whether a contractor discussing blueprints or a male client reviewing design concepts, filled her with an intense, suffocating dread. She would subtly contrive to have a colleague present or ensure meetings were always in public, open spaces. The memory of being cornered in the dim light of her apartment made being in the dark an unbearable experience; she would avoid late-night site visits or working alone in her office after sunset, instead leaving lights on throughout her house, even when her husband was home.

The need to avoid being alone extended beyond work. She found it increasingly difficult to be alone in any room or building, even her own home, constantly seeking the presence of her husband or friends. If she had to be alone, she would distract herself with endless tasks, the silence too dangerous. When memories of the event did surface, which they often did without any clear image, just a sudden rush of overwhelming emotion, Leilani would be consumed by intense guilt. She repeatedly blamed herself for what happened, replaying scenarios in her mind, convinced she could have done something differently, convinced it was somehow her fault. This rumination trapped her in a cycle of self-recrimination, further solidifying her belief that she was fundamentally flawed.

Her once vibrant social life dwindled, and even her marriage began to feel the strain of her constant unease and avoidance. She felt disconnected, the person she was before the trauma a distant memory. The weight of her symptoms finally became too much to bear. She sought help, exhausted by the relentless hypervigilance, the pervasive guilt, and the fear that she would never reclaim her life from the shadow of that terrible night. What frightened her most was the feeling that she was disappearing, becoming merely a collection of fears and avoidances, and she desperately hoped to find a way back to herself.
